In the European Union, DOW must accommodate the Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation for standardizing charging infrastructure within member states (European Commission n.d.-a.). This regulation designates the Type 2 (Mennekes) connector as the standard charging connector for Europe, whereas the U.S. commonly uses the J1772 (Type 1) connector, which works with most non-Tesla EVs and Tesla vehicles using an adapter (Besen Group 2024). New U.S. Tesla models are compatible with Type 2 connectors (Ndungu 2024), but most existing U.S. EVs equipped with the J1772 plug would require adapters for European deployments (Ellmore 2024). Participating in international standards working groups may help integrate DOW mission priorities into decision-making. 4.4 Adversarial Exploitation of Distributed Infrastructure Adversaries might exploit advanced energy technologies (such as solar PV, wind farms, or space-based systems) to camouflage or reduce the detectability of their own sensitive military assets (including weapons, drones, and communication equipment). The increasing prevalence of large-scale solar and wind installations, particularly in remote or contested regions, presents opportunities for adversaries to hide critical infrastructure or surveillance equipment. For example, solar PV could be used to conceal weaponry, making them more challenging to detect through conventional intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance methods. In addition, on-site generation assets like solar PV or wind can mask power demand signatures that would otherwise be visible on the broader grid, complicating efforts to identify unusual consumption patterns that might indicate covert operations. Offshore wind assets could conceal sensors, creating a more reliable monitoring network for adversaries. Innovative updates to U.S. detection capabilities should help counter this risk. 4.5 Increased Global Demand and Competition for Resources Individuals and government entities across the globe are adopting advanced energy technologies, increasing demand for advanced energy inputs. The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) estimates that within the next two decades, global wind energy generation will double or triple, and solar energy generation will increase to two to four times their 2024 levels (EIA 2023). Some policies abroad (e.g., the European Union’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which imposes carbon price requirements on imports of key goods) contribute to the surge in demand for advanced energy technologies (Burgess 2024). Without cost-saving technological change, competition for advanced energy assets will increase market prices for all consumers, including DOW, possibly leading to supply shortages for consumers who are less able or willing to pay higher prices. Such competitive pressures are likely to impact entire supply chains, from critical material mining to finished products.
